meta.titre: Production Possibility Frontier: scarcity, opportunity cost and economic growth
meta.sous_theme: Production possibility curves and opportunity cost

sections.contenu_markdown: Imagine that a farming region around Bafoussam can use its land and labour either to grow more maize or to grow more beans. Every extra tonne of maize means fewer tonnes of beans, and a government must also decide how much to spend on machinery that will raise output next year instead of goods to consume today. The production possibility frontier turns these choices into a simple model, and examiners use it to test scarcity, opportunity cost, efficiency and growth. This course shows how to read the curve, calculate costs from it and explain what makes it move.

items: Scarcity means that resources are limited while wants are unlimited, so choices must be made.
Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
The factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Capital goods are used to produce other goods; consumer goods are used directly to satisfy wants.

sections.titre: The production possibility frontier: meaning, shape and shifts
sections.contenu_markdown:
### What the frontier shows
A **production possibility frontier (PPF)**, also called a production possibility curve, shows the **maximum combinations of two goods (or two groups of goods) that an economy can produce in a given period** when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed and its technology is fixed.

| Position of a point | Meaning |
|---|---|
| On the frontier | Full employment and productive efficiency; more of one good is possible only by producing less of the other |
| Inside the frontier | Unemployed or inefficiently used resources; output of one or both goods can rise at no cost to the other |
| Outside the frontier | Cannot be reached with present resources and technology; it needs economic growth |

### Opportunity cost
Moving along the frontier from one point to another shows **scarcity, choice and opportunity cost**: to obtain more of one good, some of the other must be given up. The opportunity cost of one more unit of $X$ is measured in units of $Y$:

$$\text{opportunity cost of one unit of } X = \frac{\text{units of } Y \text{ given up}}{\text{units of } X \text{ gained}}$$

This is the absolute value of the slope of the frontier, called the **marginal rate of transformation**. It is measured in goods, not in money.

### Shape
- A **straight-line** frontier shows a **constant** opportunity cost: resources are equally suited to both goods.
- A frontier **bowed outward** (concave to the origin) shows **increasing opportunity cost**: resources are not equally suited to both uses, so each extra unit of one good needs the transfer of resources that are less and less suited to it.

### Economic growth
Economic growth is an **outward shift** of the frontier. It results from more resources (a labour force that grows, new discoveries, investment in capital), better quality of resources (education, training) and better technology. An **inward shift** follows war, a natural disaster or the destruction of capital. Movement from one point on the curve to another is a reallocation of resources, not growth.

An economy that devotes more of its resources to capital goods today gives up some consumer goods now, but its frontier is likely to shift further outward in the future.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives the maximum output of each good
variantes.contenu_markdown: If a country can make at most 80 units of sugar or at most 20 units of tea, the frontier is a straight line joining these two intercepts. The opportunity cost of one unit of tea is $80 \div 20 = 4$ units of sugar, and the opportunity cost of one unit of sugar is $20 \div 80 = \frac{1}{4}$ unit of tea. The opportunity cost is the same at every point of this line.

If technology improves in the production of one good only, the frontier pivots outward along that good's axis and the intercept of the other good stays where it was. If resources grow or technology improves for both goods, the frontier moves outward in both directions. A fall in unemployment moves the economy from a point inside the frontier towards it, but does not move the frontier.

variantes.nom: Uses and limits of the model
variantes.quand_utiliser: Questions that ask you to evaluate the PPF
variantes.contenu_markdown: Uses: it illustrates scarcity, choice, opportunity cost, efficiency, unemployment and growth. Limits: it simplifies the economy to two goods; it assumes fixed technology and full employment of the resources considered; it does not show which point on the curve society should choose, which depends on preferences; and the real frontier is hard to measure.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The table shows the maximum combinations of cloth and maize that an imaginary economy can produce in a year, using all its resources fully.

| Point | Cloth (thousand metres) | Maize (thousand tonnes) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 0 | 120 |
| B | 10 | 110 |
| C | 20 | 90 |
| D | 30 | 60 |
| E | 40 | 0 |

(a) Calculate the opportunity cost of one thousand metres of cloth when the economy moves from C to D.
(b) Explain why the opportunity cost of cloth rises as more cloth is produced.
(c) State what a combination of 25 cloth and 70 maize indicates.
(d) Explain the effect of better technology in both industries.

etapes.action: Read the table as points on the frontier.
etapes.justification: Every row shows the maximum maize that is possible for a given amount of cloth.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The frontier runs from A (0, 120) to E (40, 0).

etapes.action: Calculate the opportunity cost from C to D.
etapes.justification: Opportunity cost is the maize given up divided by the cloth gained.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Maize falls from 90 to 60, a loss of 30. Cloth rises from 20 to 30, a gain of 10. So the cost is $30 \div 10 =$ **3 thousand tonnes of maize** per thousand metres of cloth. The costs for A to B, B to C and D to E are 1, 2 and 6.

etapes.justification: Rising costs reveal that resources are not perfectly adaptable.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The land and workers best suited to cloth are moved first; later transfers take resources that are far better at growing maize, so more maize is lost for each extra unit of cloth. The frontier is bowed outward.

etapes.justification: Compare it with the maize that the frontier allows at 25 cloth.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The straight line joining C and D gives 75 maize at 25 cloth, and a bowed frontier lies on or above that line. 70 is below it, so the point is **inside the frontier**: resources are unemployed or used inefficiently.

etapes.action: Explain the effect of better technology.
etapes.justification: Technology raises output from the same resources, so the maximum possible rises.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The whole frontier shifts outward: more of both goods can be produced. This is economic growth and makes combinations that were unattainable before possible.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) The opportunity cost is 3 thousand tonnes of maize per thousand metres of cloth. (b) It rises because resources are not equally suited to both goods, so the frontier is concave to the origin. (c) The combination (25, 70) lies inside the frontier, which signals unemployment or inefficiency, and the economy can produce more without sacrifice. (d) Better technology in both industries shifts the frontier outward, which is economic growth.

items.erreur_markdown: "A point inside the frontier shows that the economy is growing."
items.pourquoi_faux: A point inside means resources are unemployed or wasted. Growth is an outward shift of the whole curve.
items.correction_markdown: Write that an inside point shows underuse of resources, and that growth is shown by a shift of the frontier.

items.erreur_markdown: "Producing more of one good and less of the other is economic growth."
items.pourquoi_faux: This is movement along the same frontier, a change in the allocation of resources, and total capacity is unchanged.
items.correction_markdown: Distinguish movement along the curve (reallocation, opportunity cost) from a shift of the curve (growth).

items.pourquoi_faux: On a PPF the opportunity cost of one good is the quantity of the other good given up, not its money price.
items.correction_markdown: State the answer in units of the other good, for example 3 tonnes of maize.

items.erreur_markdown: Inverting the ratio, for example giving cloth lost divided by maize gained.
items.pourquoi_faux: The opportunity cost of a unit of $X$ divides the loss of $Y$ by the gain of $X$. Inverting gives the cost of $Y$ in terms of $X$.
items.correction_markdown: Write the good whose cost you want in the denominator, and the good given up in the numerator.

items.erreur_markdown: "A point outside the curve can be reached if people work harder."
items.pourquoi_faux: Working harder is possible only if it increases resources or output per worker. With present resources and technology the point is unattainable.
items.correction_markdown: Say that a point outside needs the frontier to shift outward first.

items.enonce_markdown:
An economy can produce at most 120 tonnes of yams or at most 40 tonnes of plantains, and the frontier is a straight line.

(a) Find the opportunity cost of one tonne of plantains in terms of yams.
(b) Find the opportunity cost of one tonne of yams in terms of plantains.
(c) If it produces 60 tonnes of yams, what is the maximum quantity of plantains?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) 120 divided by 40 = **3 tonnes of yams**.

(b) 40 divided by 120 = **one third of a tonne of plantains**.

(c) Producing 60 tonnes of yams means giving up 120 - 60 = 60 tonnes of yams. At 3 tonnes of yams per tonne of plantains, 60 divided by 3 = **20 tonnes of plantains**.

items.enonce_markdown:
For each event, state whether the production possibility frontier of an economy shifts outward, shifts inward, or does not shift but the economy moves to a different position.

(a) A large new deposit of a mineral is discovered and exploited.
(b) A flood destroys roads, machines and factories.
(c) A recession leaves many workers and machines idle.
(d) A well-designed national programme of education and training raises the skills of workers over many years.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Outward shift**: the quantity of resources has increased.

(b) **Inward shift**: productive capacity has been destroyed.

(c) **No shift**: the economy moves from the frontier to a point inside it, because existing resources are not fully employed. The frontier shows capacity, which has not changed.

(d) **Outward shift** over time, because the quality of labour and its productivity rise.

Award a mark for each correct classification and a reason.

items.enonce_markdown:
The table shows an economy's frontier between capital goods and consumer goods.

| Capital goods | Consumer goods |
|---|---|
| 0 | 100 |
| 10 | 96 |
| 20 | 84 |
| 30 | 60 |
| 40 | 20 |

The economy is at 10 capital goods and 96 consumer goods and the government proposes to move to 30 capital goods and 60 consumer goods.

(a) Calculate the opportunity cost of the move and the average opportunity cost of one capital good.
(b) Explain why the opportunity cost of capital goods rises along this frontier.
(c) Evaluate the view that the move is justified.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Consumer goods fall from 96 to 60, so the opportunity cost is **36 consumer goods**. Capital goods rise by 20, so the average opportunity cost of one capital good is 36 divided by 20 = **1.8 consumer goods**.

(b) Resources are not equally suited to both uses, so successive transfers take away resources that are better at producing consumer goods; the frontier is concave to the origin (the costs between successive points are 0.4, 1.2, 2.4 and 4.0).

(c) Award marks for: for the move, more capital goods raise future productive capacity, so the frontier may shift outward and allow more of both goods later; against, 36 consumer goods are given up now, living standards fall in the short run, the benefit is uncertain and depends on how well the capital is used; the answer should reach a judgement, for example that it is justified if the future gains are large and the present sacrifice is bearable.

items_markdown: The PPF shows the maximum combinations of two goods that an economy can produce with all resources fully and efficiently used and technology fixed.
Points on the curve are efficient, points inside show unemployment or waste, and points outside cannot be reached until the economy grows.
Opportunity cost of one unit of $X$ = units of $Y$ given up divided by units of $X$ gained, and it is measured in goods, not money.
A straight frontier has constant opportunity cost; a frontier bowed outward has increasing opportunity cost.
Economic growth is an outward shift of the frontier (more or better resources, better technology); movement along the curve is reallocation.
